objective: By the end of this lesson you can teach the ELT rules and testing limits, fire extinguisher use, and survival gear for climate extremes, mountains and water, explain when to deploy a ballistic parachute or activate Emergency Autoland, brief passengers on all of it, simulate a parachute deployment, and spot and fix a learner's errors with this equipment.
why: Emergency equipment helps only if it is aboard, legal, reachable and understood by the people who may have to use it. Many reactions in an emergency are automatic, which is why training has to come before the real event [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. The habits you build decide whether the ELT battery is current, the kit is within reach and the passenger beside the parachute handle knows when, and when not, to pull it.

warmup: Think first: your learner is planning his long solo cross-country in October, over a forested ridge and along a 20-mile-wide lake. The school's airplane has a 121.5 MHz ELT. He tells you, "If anything happens the ELT brings rescuers, so I'll just take a water bottle." Which three things would you want him to check or change, and how would you get him to find them himself instead of telling him?

key_terms.def: Battery-powered transmitter that, when armed, activates by itself from crash forces and transmits for at least 48 hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
Digital ELT that can carry owner, aircraft and (newer models) position data, must be registered with NOAA, and is detected by Cospas-Sarsat satellites [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
121.5/243.0 MHz unit that emits a downward swept tone; satellites stopped monitoring these frequencies on February 1, 2009 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Portable beacon; the AIM tells pilots who do not own the aircraft to check its ELT and, as appropriate, obtain one transmitting on 406 MHz [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Substituted for a removable ELT antenna during an operational test so the signal is not broadcast [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
For 91.205(b)(12), land next to the water above the high water mark, not counting land that is sometimes under water [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
FAA-approved inflatable vest, inflated by the wearer after exiting by CO2 cartridges with an oral tube as backup, with a water-activated light [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

Supplementary flight plan information (endurance, persons on board, survival equipment, jackets, dinghies, aircraft color) kept by the filing service for search and rescue [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]] [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].
Symbols survivors lay out at least 10 feet high, such as V for require assistance and X for require medical assistance [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].
System that rockets a parachute out so it slowly lowers the whole airplane; deploying it costs the airframe [[24:345|AFH 17-11]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
System that, if activated, picks an airport, plots a course, broadcasts intentions, flies there and lands [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]].
PHAK passenger briefing list: seat belts, air, fire extinguisher, exits and survival kit, traffic and talking, your questions [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of you as an instructor

body.p: This Task covers the gear that matters after something goes wrong: the ELT, the fire extinguisher, survival gear for climate extremes, mountains and water, and, if installed, a ballistic parachute and Emergency Autoland (ACS AI.XII.D.K1 to K5). As an instructor you teach it twice: once on the ground as knowledge, and then on every flight as habits your learner copies from you.

Part 23 sets the design goal: safety and survival equipment required by the operating rules must be reliable, readily accessible, easily identifiable and clearly marked to identify its method of operation [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2535]]. Your job is to make the pilot match the equipment: knows where each item is, knows how it works, and has briefed the people who may need it.

check.a: Reliable, readily accessible, easily identifiable, and clearly marked to identify its method of operation [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2535]].

chunks.title: The ELT rule, read from 14 CFR 91.207

body.p: Teach the ELT from the current regulation, not from memory or a handbook summary. The text below is 14 CFR 91.207 as it stands today (Part 91 up to date as of 10/08/2026). Your learner should be able to find each paragraph [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

head: Paragraph
What it says
rows: (a) Who needs what

Part 135 operations, Part 121 charter flights and the Part 121/125 supplemental and commercial operator rules need an approved automatic type ELT. Other operations need an approved personal type or automatic type. Either way it must be attached and in operable condition, and a TSO-C91 ELT may not be used for new installations after June 21, 1995 [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].
(b) Mounting
Attached so the probability of crash damage is minimized; fixed and deployable automatic types as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].
(c) Battery

Replace (or recharge, if rechargeable) when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the useful life (or of the useful life of charge) set by the manufacturer has expired. The new expiration date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the maintenance record. The 50 percent rule does not apply to batteries, such as water-activated ones, that are essentially unaffected in storage [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].
(d) Inspection

Within 12 calendar months after the last inspection, for proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and a sufficient signal radiated from the antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].
(e) Ferry

A newly acquired airplane to where the ELT will be installed, or an airplane with an inoperative ELT from where it cannot be repaired to where it can; only required crewmembers aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].
(f) Exceptions a CFI meets most

(3) training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight began; (9) aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person; (10) ELT temporarily removed, with a records entry (date of removal, make, model, serial number, reason) and an "ELT not installed" placard in view of the pilot, and no operation more than 90 days after removal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

callout.text: Handbook wording to correct: the AFH 2-3 checklist line reads "ELT inspection within the last 12 months" [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. The rule says within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Teach the rule's words.

Teaching move: do not recite the battery rule. Hand the learner the logbooks, walk to the ELT, and have them find the inspection entry and the expiration date marked on the transmitter. Then ask whether today's flight is legal and which paragraph says so.

check.q: Your learner wants to take the school's airplane, whose ELT is inoperative, on a dual lesson to an airport 80 NM away, arguing that it is "training." What do you point out?
check.a: The training exception covers only training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight began; 80 NM is outside it, so the airplane needs an operable ELT [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

chunks.title: How the ELT works, how to test it, and its limits

body.p: Operations. ELTs transmit on 121.5 MHz, 243.0 MHz or 406 MHz. The 121.5 and 243.0 units are analog and emit a downward swept tone. The 406 MHz unit is digital, can be coded with owner, aircraft and (newer models) position data, sends a stronger signal, and includes a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter for the final search. The FCC and TSO-C126 require each 406 MHz ELT to be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
Limitations. Teach these four:

bullets: Analog ELTs depend on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft hearing them; Cospas-Sarsat stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz on February 1, 2009 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

SAR forces normally wait for confirmation, such as an overdue report, before acting on an analog alert, which can take hours; a 406 MHz alert can start a response in minutes [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
An armed ELT activates from crash forces and runs at least 48 hours, but it helps only if it survives the crash and is activated [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

So pilots and passengers should know how to activate it by hand and how to verify it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. Pilots who do not own the aircraft should check the installed ELT and, as appropriate, obtain a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: Testing requirements. Test per the manufacturer's instructions, preferably in a shielded or screened room or a test container, so no false alert goes out. When that cannot be done [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]:

head: ELT
When and how
rows: Analog 121.5/243 MHz

Only during the first 5 minutes after any hour; outside that window, coordinate with the nearest FAA control tower. No longer than three audible sweeps. If the antenna is removable, use a dummy load [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Digital 406 MHz
Only per the unit manufacturer's instructions [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Any ELT, in the air
Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: False alarms look exactly like real ones. Aerobatics, hard landings, ground crews and maintenance have all set ELTs off. Monitor 121.5 MHz in flight when you can, before engine shutdown at the end of each flight, and whenever the airplane is handled or moved. If you hear a signal, turn your ELT off to see if it is the source; if it was, maintenance may be needed before it is rearmed, and you should tell the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. If you hear one in flight, report where you first heard it, last heard it and heard it strongest, with your altitude and the frequency [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: Shielded first. Analog: first 5 after the hour, 3 sweeps, dummy load. 406: the maker's book. Never airborne.
Teach the post-flight listen as a checklist item, not a lecture. If the learner sees you dial 121.5 before every shutdown, they copy it; after a firm landing, make it a must.

check.q: It is 1:20 PM and no shielded test container is available. When may your learner start an operational test of the school's analog ELT without calling the tower, and how long may it run?
check.a: In the first 5 minutes after 2:00 PM, for no longer than three audible sweeps [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: Requirement. Current Part 23 standards require a means to extinguish any fire in the cabin that the pilot can easily access while seated; level 3 and 4 airplanes must also give passengers a means within the passenger compartment [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]]. Older airplanes were built to earlier rules, so check what is actually installed. Teach it like the ELT: where is it, is it secured, and can the pilot reach it with the belts on?

Operations. In the AFH the extinguisher appears in the cabin fire procedure. A cabin fire means two jobs at once: attack the fire and get on the ground as quickly as possible. Identify and shut down the faulty system. Use the extinguisher (if available) first; only then open the cabin air to purge smoke and fumes. If smoke increases with the vents open, close them at once: the fire may be in the heating system or nose baggage area, or the airflow is feeding it [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Limitations the sources give:

bullets: It does not remove the cause. Materials already ignited may keep burning after the electrical power is removed [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

The AFH engine fire procedure has no extinguisher step: shut off the fuel with the mixture and the selector instead. A fire that seems out can rekindle with changes in airflow and airspeed, and a powerless single is left with a forced landing [[24:358|AFH 18-9]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
On some airplanes, lowering the landing gear or flaps can aggravate a cabin smoke problem [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

These sources do not give the extinguishing agent, discharge time, range or by-products of a small-airplane extinguisher. The unit's label and the POH/AFM are the authority; teach learners to read them.

callout.text: On the first preflight, have the learner unclip the extinguisher, read its label aloud and secure it again. Then, belted in, ask them to touch it without looking. The F in the SAFETY briefing is its location and operation [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], and nobody briefs well what they have never handled.
Causes of fire and smoke and the full fire procedures belong to AI.XII.C. Here the question is narrower: what the extinguisher can and cannot do.

check.q: Why is a hand extinguisher not part of the AFH answer to an engine compartment fire in a single-engine airplane?
check.a: The AFH engine fire steps shut off the fuel supply with the mixture and fuel selector instead, a fire that seems out can rekindle with airflow and airspeed changes, and a powerless single is left with a forced landing [[24:358|AFH 18-9]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

chunks.title: Gear for climate extremes and mountainous terrain

body.p: The general rule: for flight over uninhabited land, take survival equipment for the type of climate and terrain, and know how to use it [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. On a trip over remote areas, ask during planning whether appropriate clothing, water and survival gear are aboard for a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]] [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. The AIH personal minimums checklist carries the same lines: survival gear appropriate for the flight and terrain, and clothing suitable for preflight and flight [[25:207|AIH D-2]].

head: Sub-item
What the sources tie to it
Why
rows: Climate extremes: hot (K3a)

Water: carry an ample supply and drink at frequent intervals whether thirsty or not [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]; the PHAK guide is two to four quarts every 24 hours, with a container to measure intake [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. Under a canopy or roof window, light-colored, porous clothing and a hat [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].
Thirst starts only at about a 1.5 quart deficit (2 percent of body weight) and a sip turns it off; heatstroke may be recognized only on collapse [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Climate extremes: cold (K3a)

Clothing for the ground, not the heated cabin [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. A winter kit: the AIM recommends minimum summer and winter kits for remote areas, notes they are required by law for flight into sparsely settled areas of Canada and Alaska, and says to keep the kit in one easily reachable container [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

A landing in snow is flown like a ditching, with the same risk of whiteout and lost depth perception [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. In snow, signals can be tramped or shoveled, and the depressions look black from the air [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].
Mountainous terrain (K3b)

A filed flight plan, a route over populated areas and well-known passes, and enough altitude to glide to a safe landing if the engine fails [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]]; a planned escape route with room for a 180 degree turn [[34:163|AIM 7-6-7]]. Then the climate kit for the elevation and season.
Flat fields for forced landings are practically nonexistent, and winds and clouds change fast [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]]. The RMH lists mountains as an environment hazard [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

body.p: Teaching angle: the sources give principles, not a packing list. Make the learner build the list for the actual route, season and passengers, and defend each item against those principles. That is a scenario: the learner plans the route, destination, weather, NOTAMs and possible emergency procedures [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

callout.text: Cold weather over mountains adds a hidden terrain risk: flying into colder air, the altimeter reads too high, so true clearance over the peaks is less than indicated [[28:107|AWH 8-13]].

check.q: Your learner packs a winter kit but splits it between the rear seat pocket and the aft baggage area. What does the AIM say about how a kit should be packed?
check.a: Assembled in one container that is easily reachable and preferably floatable [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

body.p: Overwater operations: if a forced landing occurs at sea, survival depends on crew proficiency in emergency procedures and on having effective water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. Over water there may be no suitable surface for an emergency landing at all [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

head: Flight
What the rule requires
rows: Part 91, not for hire, small single
No flotation rule; 91.205(b)(12) applies only for hire, so the gear is the PIC's decision, guided by the AIM [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]] [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].
For hire, over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and, unless under Part 121, at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
Contrast: large and turbojet multiengine airplanes (Part 91 subpart F)

More than 50 NM from shore: a life preserver or approved flotation means for each occupant. More than 30 minutes or 100 NM, whichever is less: life preservers with survivor locator lights, liferafts, pyrotechnics and a portable survival radio [[60:530|14 CFR 91.509(a)]] [[60:531|14 CFR 91.509(b)]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]].

body.p: Which flotation gear: FAA-approved life vests (TSO-C13E) are inflatable. Bulky Coast Guard type PFDs can block the narrow exits of small aircraft. The wearer inflates the vest after exiting, mainly by CO2 cartridges with an oral tube as backup, and the vest has a water-activated light. Passengers must be briefed on where the vests are and how to use them [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

Help and signals: if a ditching is coming, make every effort to ditch near a surface vessel; an FAA facility may get the nearest vessel's position from a Coast Guard Rescue Coordination Center [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Over tropical oceans, a cumulus top higher than its neighbors usually marks an island, so head toward it [[28:211|AWH 17-5]].

callout.text: Wear the vest uninflated and inflate it outside [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]. Teach the reason in the seat: point at the door and ask the learner how an inflated vest would get through it.

body.p: Ditching technique (reading the swell, picking the heading, touchdown attitude) is in CA.IX.D and in emergency approach and landing (AI.XII.B).

check.q: Which two items does 91.205(b)(12) require on a for-hire flight beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, and who is exempt from the second one?
check.a: Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device; the pyrotechnic item does not apply to aircraft operating under Part 121 [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

body.p: The ACS states this risk element as "Survival gear (water, clothing, shelter) for 48 to 72 hours" (ACS AI.XII.D.R1). None of these sources explains where that window comes from or gives a kit list for it. What they do give is why the first days decide the outcome:

bullets: From the National SAR Plan: an injured survivor's life expectancy decreases as much as 80 percent during the first 24 hours, and uninjured survivors' chances diminish rapidly after the first 3 days [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
Without a flight plan, 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

With a VFR flight plan, a search starts if you do not respond within one-half hour after your ETA at the final destination, which is why the AIM says to file only to the first intended landing and refile each leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
An ELT transmits for at least 48 hours, if it survives and activates [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: Manage the risk from both ends. Mitigation reduces the likelihood or the predicted severity of a hazard [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]. A forced landing far from help may be remote in likelihood but catastrophic in severity, which the matrix rates serious; serious risks call for more mitigation before a go [[30:34|RMH 4-1]] [[30:35|RMH 4-2]] [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

head: Lever
How it cuts the risk
rows: Shorten the wait
File and follow a flight plan, and tell someone your route [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]; carry a 406 MHz ELT or PLB [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Tell rescuers what you carry

Item 19 records endurance, persons on board, survival equipment, jackets, dinghies and aircraft color, and stays with the filing service for search and rescue [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]] [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].
Last until they come
Water, clothing and shelter for the climate and terrain, in a kit that is easy to reach [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
Be easy to find
Stay with the aircraft unless you have good reason to think you will not be found, and prepare signals [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: Application, labeled as such: water, clothing and shelter for 48 to 72 hours means sizing the kit for a slow rescue, not the best case. With the PHAK guide of two to four quarts per person every 24 hours [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]], the water adds up fast, and so does its weight. That is a weight and balance discussion, not a reason to leave the water behind.

callout.text: Teach R1 with a timeline, not a list. Draw a line from takeoff to 72 hours and have the learner mark the flight plan ETA, ETA plus 30 minutes, the 36-hour no-flight-plan alert and the 48-hour ELT minimum. Then ask what keeps each passenger alive in each gap.

check.q: Your learner files one VFR flight plan for a three-leg trip with a single ETA at the last stop. Why is that a survival-gear problem and not just paperwork?
check.a: A mishap on the first leg might not start a search until 30 minutes after the final ETA, so the kit has to cover a longer wait; the AIM says to file to the first intended landing and refile each leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

chunks.title: Ballistic parachutes: when to deploy and what to brief

body.p: A ballistic parachute rockets a canopy out so it slowly lowers the airplane [[24:345|AFH 17-11]]. Deployed within an acceptable flight regime it prevents injuries and saves lives, and occupants usually survive the impact with minor or no injuries, but the airframe is lost. Some designs add landing gear and seats built to absorb vertical impact forces [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

When to deploy. The AFH's examples of conditions that would qualify: a catastrophic loss of controllability due to a collision or mechanical failure, an actual loss of control, or pilot incapacitation. The limits of the acceptable flight regime are the manufacturer's; pilots should study the information from manufacturers and suppliers and follow it [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

Passenger briefings. Brief any passenger with access to a deployment mechanism on the conditions for a safe deployment; generally a passenger would deploy only if the pilot were incapacitated. At a minimum, also brief the basic sequence of steps. Once on the ground, the deployed parachute and surface winds create hazards, so occupants should know the evacuation procedure [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

head: Risk in using the system (R2)
How you teach the learner to manage it
rows: Hesitating to save the airplane

The AFH says the desire to save the airplane leads pilots to ignore basic airmanship, and there are times to sacrifice the airplane so the occupants walk away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Reluctance to accept the emergency brings indecision [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Settle the triggers on the ground, before flight.
Deploying outside the regime
Know the manufacturer's limits before flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Arming and disarming errors

Follow the manufacturer's arming and disarming procedures before and after flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]] (ACS Appendix 3); preflight the mounts, safety pin and flag, and activation handle and cable [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
A passenger who pulls at the wrong time
Brief the conditions, and that a passenger normally deploys only if the pilot is incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Hazards after touchdown
Brief the canopy and wind hazards and the evacuation plan [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

callout.text: Most standard airworthiness airplanes do not have these systems, so transition training should cover the system's operation and limitations [[24:345|AFH 17-11]]. Use the manufacturer's training material for the make you teach in.

check.q: Why should the parachute deployment triggers be settled on the ground, not in the moment?
check.a: Because the desire to save the airplane leads pilots to poor choices in an emergency [[24:351|AFH 18-2]], and the AFH already names qualifying conditions (catastrophic loss of controllability, actual loss of control, pilot incapacitation) that can be agreed in advance [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: S3 asks you to simulate ballistic parachute deployment procedures, if equipped. The ACS allows simulation and briefing only, never actual deployment (ACS Appendix 3). The sources give no universal checklist, handle force or speed limits; the steps below are the parts the AFH and ACS give, and the make-specific steps come from the manufacturer's procedures [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: 1. Preflight: check the mounts, safety pin and flag, and the activation handle and cable [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
2. Arm the system per the manufacturer before flight (ACS Appendix 3) [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
3. Brief any passenger who can reach the handle on the deployment conditions and the basic sequence of steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

4. In the simulation, name the trigger aloud (for example, "controls jammed after a midair, I cannot control the airplane") and confirm it fits one of the AFH's qualifying conditions [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
5. Call out and point to each step of the manufacturer's deployment checklist, without pulling (ACS Appendix 3).
6. Talk through touchdown and evacuation: the canopy and surface wind are hazards [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
7. After flight, disarm per the manufacturer (ACS Appendix 3) [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: How to teach it: first the learner tells while you do, then the learner tells and does. Narration lets you hear a misunderstanding and fix it before the learner is busy flying, and primacy means the first version should be the right one [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application (the sources give no ground-training procedure): agree before the lesson that in any simulation the hand points at the handle and never closes on it, and say "simulated" before each step. Check the manufacturer's training guidance for the system's ground state.

check.q: During a simulated deployment your learner says "pull" and reaches for the handle. What sets the limit, and what should she do instead?
check.a: ACS Appendix 3 allows simulation and briefing, not actual deployment, and the AFH says to follow the manufacturer's procedures; she should call and point to each manufacturer checklist step without pulling [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

chunks.title: Emergency Autoland: when to activate and what to brief

body.p: What it is. An Emergency Autoland system, if activated, determines an optimal airport, plots a course, broadcasts the aircraft's intentions, flies to the airport, lands and, depending on the model, shuts down the engines [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]]. In a pilot incapacitation it may assume operation of the aircraft and deviate to meet that emergency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

When it activates. If it senses erratic flying it stabilizes the airplane and checks for pilot responsiveness; without further input it starts an emergency descent, and if the pilot still does not respond, an automated landing. A pilot or a passenger can also activate it manually [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Application: teach passengers that the trigger to press it is a pilot who is unresponsive or clearly unable to fly, and teach pilots that manual activation is theirs to use too.

head: What EAL does
What it does not do
rows: Broadcasts on the last selected frequency and 121.5 MHz in a synthesized voice, squawks 7700, then pauses 25 seconds so ATC can work conflicting traffic [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]
Detect and avoid other aircraft [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]
Within 12 miles of the runway and at or below 12,000 ft MSL, talks on tower frequency or CTAF and keeps reporting by ADS-B, with a one-minute-out call [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]
Receive or react to ATC instructions or NOTAMs [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]
Chooses an airport by weather, wind, runway length and towered status, only among airports with an RNAV or GPS approach [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]
Avoid MOAs, special use airspace, restricted areas or TFRs [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]
Uses obstacle and terrain databases; with no GPS it flies straight and does not try to land until GPS returns [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]
Turn on aircraft lights [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]

body.p: Brief passengers on where the activation control is, when to use it, and what happens next: the airplane will fly and talk by itself. Controllers are told to assume its transmissions will not be acknowledged [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]]. The exact activation steps come from the POH/AFM supplement.

callout.text: Risk of use (R3): the system cannot see traffic or airspace [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]. Application: teach it as a last resort for incapacitation, never as a reason to fly while impaired.

check.q: Your passenger asks whether the autoland will steer around a TFR on its way to the airport. Your answer?
check.a: No. Current EAL capabilities do not include avoiding MOAs, special use airspace, restricted areas or TFRs [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

body.p: The briefing the rule requires: before takeoff the PIC must ensure each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)]]. The rest of S2 comes from guidance: the SAFETY list includes the fire extinguisher's location and operation, and the emergency/survival kit's location and contents [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

head: Equipment
What the passenger needs to know
rows: Fire extinguisher
Where it is and how it operates [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Survival kit
Where it is and what is in it [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
ELT
How to activate it by hand and check that it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Life vests
Where they are and how to use them; inflate only after exiting [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]
Ballistic parachute
Conditions for deployment (normally pilot incapacitation), the basic steps, and evacuation under a canopy in wind [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]
Emergency Autoland
When to activate it and that a passenger can do it manually [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]

body.p: How to teach it: model the briefing on every flight, then hand it over. The learner gives it to you as if you were a nervous first-time passenger, then to a real passenger while you watch. Have the passenger touch each item, not just look at it. Telling first and then doing builds the habit [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: tie the briefing to the route. Over water, the vests come first; over winter mountains, the kit and clothing; in a parachute airplane, the handle. A briefing that never changes is one passengers stop hearing.

check.q: Your learner briefs the ELT as "it turns itself on in a crash." What did he leave out that the AIM says passengers should know?
check.a: How to activate it manually and how to verify it is functioning and transmitting after a crash or manual activation [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: an emergency equipment lesson

body.p: Timing. Introduce emergency equipment once the learner is at home with normal operations; introduced then, emergency procedures are less likely to discourage or frighten [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. Do not leave it late, though: many reactions in an emergency are automatic, so the training must come first [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
A lesson flow that fits this Task:

bullets: 1. Records and airplane: the learner finds the ELT inspection entry and battery date, and states whether 91.207 is met [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].
2. Equipment walk: extinguisher (read the label, reach it belted in), kit, vests, and the parachute handle and EAL control if installed.

3. Scenario planning: give a real route and season. The learner plans the route, weather, NOTAMs and possible emergency procedures [[25:31|AIH 1-27]], picks gear for each environment, and fills in Item 19 [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].
4. Briefing: the learner briefs you, then a real passenger.
5. In flight: a simulated problem that tests decisions, such as a parachute talk-through or a simulated incapacitation discussion in an EAL airplane [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

6. After landing: the 121.5 MHz listen before shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]], disarm the parachute per the manufacturer (ACS Appendix 3), and a debrief on which risks the learner named without prompting.

body.p: Scenario-based training puts these items inside realistic flights instead of a list to memorize; once learned, procedures are folded into realistic scenarios [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

callout.text: Teaching risk: you can create the "save the airplane" trap yourself. The AFH says a pilot conditioned in training to always find a relatively safe field when the instructor closes the throttle may ignore basic airmanship to avoid damaging the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Mix in simulated emergencies over poor terrain, and in parachute airplanes talk through the deploy decision.

Never activate a real ELT, extinguisher, autoland or parachute to show how it works. Simulate (ACS Appendix 3), and test the ELT only as the AIM allows [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. A live EAL activation would squawk 7700 and broadcast on 121.5 MHz [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

check.q: Why does the AIH suggest waiting until the learner knows normal operations before teaching emergency equipment, and why not wait too long?
check.a: Introduced after normal operations, emergency procedures are less likely to discourage or frighten the learner [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]; but many emergency responses are automatic, so they must be trained before a real emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Cannot find the ELT dates
Says "maintenance handles that" or guesses
Back to the records and the transmitter label; 91.207(c) and (d) [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]
Misusing an ELT exception
Plans a trip beyond 50 NM with the ELT out, or keeps flying past 90 days after removal
Read (f)(3) and (f)(10) word by word together [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]
Testing the ELT wrong
Tests at 20 past the hour, lets it run, or wants to try it in flight
Analog: first 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps; 406: manufacturer only; never airborne [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Skipping the 121.5 listen
Shuts down after a firm landing without listening
Make it a checklist item before shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Extinguisher never handled
Cannot reach it belted in or explain how it works
Locate, reach and read the label every preflight [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Vents before extinguisher
In a cabin fire talk-through, opens the air first
Extinguisher first, then vents; close them if smoke increases [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Kit buried or mismatched
Gear under bags in the aft baggage area, or the same kit for desert and snow
One easily reached container [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]; gear for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]
Inflating a vest inside
Passenger briefed to pull the tab "when we go down"
Wear it uninflated; inflate after exiting [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]
No flight plan, or one long one
"I'll just text my spouse"
File, refile each leg, close on arrival [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]
Hesitating to deploy
In a scenario, keeps fighting a jammed-control airplane
Rehearse the qualifying conditions on the ground [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]; the airplane is expendable [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]
Parachute arming slips
Skips the pin, flag, handle and cable check, or leaves the system armed after flight
Arm and disarm per the manufacturer before and after flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]; preflight items [[24:345|AFH 17-11]]
Passenger not briefed on parachute or EAL
Briefing ends at the doors
Add deployment conditions and basic steps, and when and how to activate EAL [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]

body.p: Spotting errors works best when the learner thinks aloud: you can then tell whether a mistake comes from a misconception or from a simple lack of skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: In a scenario, your learner keeps trying to glide a parachute-equipped airplane toward a distant field after a midair jammed the controls. Which error is it and how do you fix it?
check.a: Hesitating to deploy: an actual loss of control after a collision is one of the AFH's qualifying conditions [[24:371|AFH 18-22]], and the desire to save the airplane is a known trap [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]; rehearse the triggers on the ground.

scenario.title: Final checkout trip in a parachute and autoland airplane, January
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI giving a transition checkout to a private pilot who just bought a four-seat composite single with a ballistic parachute, Emergency Autoland and a 406 MHz ELT. Next week he plans to fly his wife and teenage son 250 NM in January across a mountain range and then along a large reservoir to a lake-house strip, and he wants you aboard as the last part of the checkout. On the ramp, you see that the ELT battery expiration date marked on the transmitter was last month.

questions.q: What does the battery date mean for the trip, and what is the fix?
questions.a: The battery had to be replaced (or recharged) by the time 50 percent of its useful life expired, so the ELT does not meet 91.207(c) [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]; a 250 NM trip is not covered by the 50 NM training exception [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]. Replace it and mark the new date on the transmitter and in the maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

questions.q: How do you get him to choose the survival gear himself instead of handing him a list?
questions.a: Run it as a scenario: he plans the route, weather, NOTAMs and possible emergency procedures [[25:31|AIH 1-27]] and picks gear for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]: winter clothing and a kit in one reachable container [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]], a route over passes with gliding altitude and an escape route [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]] [[34:163|AIM 7-6-7]], and vests for the reservoir leg [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

questions.q: The flight is not for hire. Are life vests required for the reservoir leg?
questions.a: No rule requires them; 91.205(b)(12) applies only to for-hire flights beyond power-off gliding distance from shore [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. But survival at sea depends on effective water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]], so carrying inflatable vests, worn uninflated, is the safer choice [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

questions.q: His wife will sit next to the parachute handle and the EAL control. What does he brief her?
questions.a: The conditions for a safe deployment (normally only if he is incapacitated), the basic steps, and evacuation with the canopy and wind hazards; when and how to activate EAL manually [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]; how to activate the ELT and check it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]; and the extinguisher and survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: He says that over the mountains he would ride a dead engine down rather than "waste the parachute." How do you respond?
questions.a: The AFH warns that the desire to save the airplane leads to poor choices and that sometimes the airplane should be sacrificed so the occupants walk away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Deployment decisions depend on the manufacturer's conditions and flight regime, which he must study before the trip [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. The sources do not say when an engine failure alone qualifies, so the manufacturer's guidance decides.

questions.q: How does he widen the 48 to 72 hour margin (ACS AI.XII.D.R1) for his family?
questions.a: File a flight plan, to the first landing with a refile for each leg, and close it on arrival [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]; list survival equipment, jackets, persons on board and aircraft color in Item 19 [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]]; keep the 406 MHz ELT registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]; and carry water, clothing and shelter for the season and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

skills.do: Identify appropriate equipment and personal gear (ACS AI.XII.D.S1). There is no numeric tolerance. Expect to walk the records and airplane as if teaching: find the ELT inspection and battery dates and state whether 91.207 is met, show the extinguisher and explain its use, and choose survival gear for a route and season the examiner names, saying why each item fits the climate, terrain or water.
skills.practice: Do the records-and-airplane walk on every airplane you will teach in [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Pack a kit for your local terrain and season from the AIM and PHAK principles [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]] [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]], and fill in Item 19 for a practice flight plan [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].

skills.do: Brief passengers on proper use of on-board emergency equipment and survival gear (ACS AI.XII.D.S2). No numeric tolerance: give the briefing to the examiner as if to a passenger, touching each item (belts, extinguisher, exits, kit, ELT, vests, and the parachute and EAL if installed), then explain how you teach a learner to give it.
skills.practice: Write a card from the SAFETY list [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] plus the equipment table in this lesson, add the parachute and EAL items [[24:371|AFH 18-22]], and brief real passengers until it is short and natural.

skills.do: Simulate ballistic parachute deployment procedures, if equipped (ACS AI.XII.D.S3). Only in a parachute-equipped airplane. No numeric tolerance: arm and disarm per the manufacturer, state the deployment conditions, and call and point to the manufacturer's deployment steps without pulling. Testing is by simulation and briefing, never deployment (ACS Appendix 3).
skills.practice: Chair-fly the manufacturer's checklist in the airplane, narrating each step, and rehearse the AFH triggers with scenarios such as a midair or jammed controls [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.XII.D.S4). No numeric tolerance: the examiner may play a learner who tests the ELT at 20 past the hour, opens the vents before using the extinguisher, or hesitates to deploy. Name the error, its source, and the fix.
skills.practice: Use the error table in the last chunk as flash cards: for each row say what you would see and the fix with its source [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

quiz.q: Under 91.207(a), which of these operations needs an approved automatic type ELT, with no personal type allowed?
options: A Part 91 aerial photo flight for hire
A dual cross-country lesson beyond 50 NM
A Part 135 on-demand charter flight
A private flight with three passengers aboard
quiz.why: Part 135 operations (and certain Part 121 and 125 operations) need an approved automatic type; other operations may use a personal or automatic type [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

quiz.q: An ELT has a water-activated battery. Which part of the 91.207(c) battery rule does not apply to it?
options: The 50 percent of useful life replacement limit
The 1 cumulative hour of use limit
Marking the new date on the transmitter
Entering the new date in the records
quiz.why: Paragraph (c)(2), the 50 percent rule, does not apply to batteries such as water-activated ones that are essentially unaffected during storage [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

quiz.q: What does a 406 MHz ELT carry to help searchers in the final, terminal phase of a search?
options: A strobe on the tail that flashes on impact
A satellite voice link to the rescue center
A downward swept tone on 243.0 MHz only
A low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter
quiz.why: 406 MHz ELTs include a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter for the terminal search phase [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: An analog ELT with a removable antenna must be tested in the airplane. What does the AIM say to do about the antenna?
options: Substitute a dummy load during the test
Leave it on and limit the test to one sweep
Remove it and test the unit with no load
Leave it on but test only near a tower
quiz.why: If the antenna is removable, a dummy load should be substituted during test procedures [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: Which extinguisher fact will your learner NOT find in the AFH, PHAK or Part 23 pages used in this lesson, so it must come from the unit's label and POH?
options: That it is used before the cabin vents open
That the pilot must reach it while seated
Which agent it holds and how long it discharges
That its location belongs in the briefing
quiz.why: The AFH gives the cabin fire order [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], Part 23 the seated reach [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]] and the PHAK the briefing item [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; none gives agent or discharge time, so use the label and POH.

quiz.q: For hot weather in an airplane with a canopy or roof window, what does the AIH suggest wearing?
options: Dark, tightly woven clothing and gloves
A long-sleeved flight suit, sleeves down
Light-colored, porous clothing and a hat
Whatever is comfortable with vents closed
quiz.why: Light-colored, porous clothing and a hat help protect from the sun, and a well-ventilated flight deck helps dissipate heat [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

quiz.q: Which route does the AIM recommend for a light airplane crossing mountains?
options: The most direct line at the highest altitude
Along the ridgelines to use the updrafts there
Through the valleys, low and under the clouds
Over populated areas and well-known passes
quiz.why: Route over populated areas and well-known mountain passes, with enough altitude to glide to a safe landing if the engine fails [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]].

quiz.q: According to an Air Force review quoted in the AIM, how long normally passes before family concern starts an alert for a pilot with no flight plan?
options: 30 minutes
36 hours
24 hours
72 hours
quiz.why: "36 hours normally pass before family concern initiates an (alert)" [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, where do the limits of the acceptable flight regime for a parachute deployment come from?
options: 14 CFR 91.207 and the ELT rules
The pilot's personal minimums
ACS Appendix 3 for each airplane
The manufacturer's and supplier's guidance
quiz.why: Deploy within an acceptable flight regime, and study and follow the guidance from the system's manufacturers and suppliers [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

quiz.q: An Emergency Autoland system has just made its first automated broadcast. What does it do next?
options: Pauses 25 seconds so ATC can move traffic
Turns on all of the exterior lights at once
Requests a landing clearance from the tower
Climbs to 12,000 ft MSL to find GPS
quiz.why: After the initial broadcast the system pauses for 25 seconds to allow ATC to communicate with potential conflicting traffic [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: The school's ELT was removed for repair on March 2, with the records entry and the placard done. On June 10 a learner books a dual lesson in the practice area 15 NM from the airport and back. What applies?
options: Not allowed: the 90-day removal limit ran out on May 31, so it is grounded
Allowed: local training within 50 NM is excepted
Allowed only under a special ferry permit to a repair station
Allowed only if the placard is moved into the learner's view
final_quiz.why: March 2 plus 90 days is May 31, so (f)(10) no longer covers it, but paragraph (a) does not apply to training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

final_quiz.q: A rechargeable ELT battery has a useful life of charge of 18 months set by the manufacturer. It was recharged in January 2026 and has not been used. When must it be recharged again?
options: September 2027
January 2027
April 2026
October 2026
final_quiz.why: 50 percent of 18 months is 9 months; January 2026 plus 9 months is October 2026 [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

final_quiz.q: On a cross-country you hear an ELT tone on 121.5 MHz. Which report does the AIM ask you to give the nearest air traffic facility?
options: Your position at first and last signal and at maximum strength, with altitude and frequency
Only the time you first heard it, so ATC can start a search clock for the overdue aircraft
The aircraft color and call sign you think it belongs to
Nothing until the tone has lasted three audible sweeps
final_quiz.why: Report your position when first heard, when last heard and at maximum signal strength, plus altitudes and frequency [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: In a cabin smoke talk-through, your learner uses the extinguisher, opens the vents and the smoke clears. She then lowers full flaps early "to get down fast" and the smoke returns. What does the AFH note?
options: Flaps have no effect on cabin airflow in light single-engine airplanes
On some airplanes, lowering gear or flaps can aggravate cabin smoke
Full flaps are required before opening foul weather windows
Smoke returning always means an engine compartment fire
final_quiz.why: The AFH says that on some airplanes lowering the landing gear and/or wing flaps can aggravate a cabin smoke problem [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: Winter, over wide snow-covered open terrain, the engine quits. How does the AFH say to fly the snow landing?
options: Gear down and full flaps so the airplane absorbs energy at the slowest speed
Like a ditching, same configuration, watching for whiteout and lost depth
At normal approach speed to keep the nose out of deep snow
Into the sun, so shadows show the surface texture clearly
final_quiz.why: A landing in snow should be executed like a ditching, in the same configuration and with the same regard for loss of depth perception (whiteout) [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: You fly three passengers for hire to an island 20 NM offshore in a four-seat single, beyond power-off gliding distance from shore for part of the trip. What does Part 91 require?
options: Liferafts with locator lights and a portable survival radio
Nothing, because the airplane is a single-engine landplane
Approved flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
Coast Guard foam PFDs for each passenger, stowed under the seats
final_quiz.why: 91.205(b)(12) requires approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]; liferafts come from 91.509, which applies to large and turbojet multiengine airplanes [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A corporate pilot asks why his Part 91 turbojet twin must carry liferafts on a 150 NM overwater leg while your single did not. Which rule explains it?
options: 91.509, which applies to large and turbojet multiengine airplanes under subpart F
91.207(a)(1), which requires automatic type ELTs for turbojets
91.205(b)(12), which sets liferaft rules for every Part 91 airplane over water
91.107(a), which requires liferaft briefings for all flights beyond 100 NM from shore
final_quiz.why: Subpart F covers large and turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]]; beyond 30 minutes or 100 NM, whichever is less, 91.509 requires liferafts and other equipment [[60:530|14 CFR 91.509(a)]] [[60:531|14 CFR 91.509(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner files a domestic VFR flight plan. Which Item 19 entries does the AIM list as the minimum required?
options: Survival equipment, life jackets, dinghies and the emergency radios carried
Fuel on board, alternate airport and pilot certificate number
Endurance, persons on board, pilot name and contact, and aircraft color
ELT type, its registration number and the battery date
final_quiz.why: Minimum Item 19 entries for a domestic flight are endurance, persons on board, pilot name and contact information, and color of aircraft [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these does the AFH list as an example of a condition that would qualify for ballistic parachute deployment?
options: A rough-running engine while still within gliding range of an airport
Pilot incapacitation, with a briefed passenger at the handle
A low fuel warning 10 miles from the destination
An unforecast cloud layer under a VFR cruise altitude
final_quiz.why: The AFH examples are catastrophic loss of controllability from a collision or mechanical failure, actual loss of control, or pilot incapacitation; a passenger would generally deploy only if the pilot were incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: After a deployment, your airplane is down in a field with a strong surface wind. What does the AFH flag, and what should have been briefed?
options: Fuel vapor under the canopy; stay inside until help comes
Nothing; the gear and seats absorb all the remaining risk
The deployed parachute and surface winds; the evacuation procedure
The ELT battery limit; turn the ELT off to save the battery
final_quiz.why: Once on the ground there are hazards from a deployed parachute and surface winds, and occupants should know the procedures for evacuation [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: An EAL-equipped airplane whose pilot is incapacitated is diverting toward a towered airport. A controller wants to vector it. What should the controller assume?
options: The system will read back and comply with any vectors given
The system will acknowledge only on 121.5 MHz
A passenger will be flying and can follow vectors
Its transmissions will not acknowledge the controller
final_quiz.why: Though the system broadcasts its intentions, the controller should assume transmissions to the aircraft will not be acknowledged [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]]; it does not react to ATC instructions [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

final_quiz.q: In every simulated forced landing you gave, your learner found a good field. Now, in a parachute scenario over dense forest, she stretches the glide toward a distant clearing. What does the AFH say causes this?
options: Startle response from a lack of instrument training
The desire to save the airplane, conditioned by always finding a safe field in training
Get-there-itis from external pressure to reach the destination
Spatial disorientation from flying over a featureless forest
final_quiz.why: A pilot conditioned in training to expect a relatively safe landing area whenever the instructor closed the throttle may ignore basic airmanship to avoid damaging the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

final_quiz.q: The school's 406 MHz ELT needs an operational test in the airplane and no shielded room is available. What does the AIM allow?
options: Testing only per the unit manufacturer's instructions
Testing within the first 5 minutes after the hour, for three sweeps
Testing in flight above 3,000 ft AGL, then reporting it
Testing at any time if the tower is told first
final_quiz.why: Digital 406 MHz ELTs should only be tested in accordance with the unit manufacturer's instructions; airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

takeaways: Teach the ELT from 14 CFR 91.207 itself: automatic type for Part 135, battery at more than 1 cumulative hour or 50 percent of useful life, inspection within 12 calendar months, and narrow exceptions.
Analog ELTs wait for someone to hear them; 406 MHz ELTs reach satellites. Test only as the AIM allows, never airborne, and listen on 121.5 before every shutdown.
The extinguisher is for cabin fires and is used before the vents open; its agent and limits come from its label and POH.
Gear follows the route: water and sun protection for heat, a winter kit for cold, passes and glide altitude for mountains, inflatable vests worn uninflated over water.
R1 is a timeline: shorten the wait with a flight plan and a 406 MHz beacon, and last 48 to 72 hours with water, clothing and shelter.
Parachute and autoland decisions are made on the ground: triggers, regime, arming, and who may pull or press, briefed to the person in that seat.
Simulate, never deploy or activate, and build every item into the learner's normal flow so it is automatic before it is needed.
cfi_notes: Handbook vs. rule: the AFH 2-3 sample checklist says "ELT inspection within the last 12 months" [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]; 14 CFR 91.207(d) says within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Teach the CFR wording.

The PHAK 9-9 battery summary leaves out the requirement to mark the new expiration date on the transmitter and in the maintenance record, and the exception for batteries unaffected in storage [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Teach the full current text of 91.207(c) [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

The AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary still defines an ELT as operating on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]], while AIM 6-2-4 adds the 406 MHz units that satellites detect today [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. Teach 6-2-4.

91.207 says nothing about how or when to test an ELT; the testing times and the "no airborne tests" line are AIM guidance [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]] on top of the manufacturer's instructions. Say which is rule and which is guidance.

The ACS asks for gear for 48 to 72 hours (R1), but none of these sources explains that window. The AIM survival odds and the 48-hour ELT minimum support it [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]] [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]; label anything beyond that as your own reasoning.

The AIM's kit and life vest advice sits in the seaplane safety paragraph [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]. The vest and one-container principles apply to landplanes too, and 91.205(b)(12) applies to any aircraft for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

Watch your own simulated forced landings: always closing the throttle over a good field conditions the "save the airplane" reflex the AFH warns about [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Vary the terrain, and in parachute airplanes talk through the deploy decision.

Do not activate an EAL system for a demonstration unless the manufacturer provides a training mode: activation squawks 7700 and broadcasts on 121.5 MHz [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. The sources are silent on training use.

The AIH pulls in two directions on timing: introduce emergencies after normal operations [[25:161|AIH 8-3]], but train before responses must be automatic [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. In practice, cover the equipment early on the ground and add scenarios as skill grows.
gaps: No source here gives fire extinguisher agents, discharge times, effective range or toxic by-products for small airplanes; use the unit's label and the POH/AFM.
No source gives a 48 to 72 hour kit list, shelter guidance, cold-weather clothing list or food amounts for Part 91; the instructor and the route decide.
Ballistic parachute arming steps, handle force, speed and altitude limits, and EAL activation steps are manufacturer specific; the AFH gives only general guidance [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
The sources do not say whether an engine failure over hostile terrain, by itself, qualifies for deployment; the manufacturer's guidance decides.
How to use a pyrotechnic device, signal mirror or personal locator beacon, and how to register a PLB, are not covered; follow the device instructions.
Test procedures for 406 MHz ELTs are left to each manufacturer [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

activities.title: True or false: reading 91.207
activities.intro: Decide if each statement matches the current rule.

cards.s: A TSO-C91 ELT may be used for a new installation today if it is operable.
cards.why: False. After June 21, 1995 an ELT meeting TSO-C91 may not be used for new installations [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

cards.s: A rechargeable ELT battery is due when 50 percent of its useful life of charge has expired.
An airplane ferried to a shop under 91.207(e) may carry a mechanic who is not a required crewmember.
cards.why: False. No person other than required crewmembers may be carried on a ferry flight under (e) [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

cards.s: An airplane equipped to carry not more than one person is excepted from 91.207(a).
Fixed automatic type ELTs should be mounted as far forward as practicable.
cards.why: False. Fixed and deployable automatic types go as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].

cards.s: The ELT inspection includes operation of the controls and the crash sensor.
cards.why: True, one of the four items in 91.207(d) [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].

activities.title: ELT numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: An ELT transmitted for 25 minutes after a hard landing and 40 more minutes during maintenance. By how many minutes has it passed the 1 cumulative hour battery limit?
items.why: 25 + 40 = 65 minutes; 65 - 60 = 5 minutes over, so the battery must be replaced or recharged [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

items.q: An ELT was removed for repair 61 days ago, with the records entry and placard in place. How many more days may the airplane be operated under the removal exception?
items.why: The limit is 90 days after initial removal: 90 - 61 = 29 days [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

items.q: Your learner finishes the preflight at 1412 and wants to test the analog ELT in the airplane without calling the tower. How many minutes must she wait for the earliest allowed start?
items.why: Analog tests belong in the first 5 minutes after any hour, so the next window opens at 1500: 1500 - 1412 = 48 minutes [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

items.q: An ELT battery has a manufacturer useful life of 5 years and is never used. How many months after installation is it due?
items.why: 50 percent of 5 years = 2.5 years = 2.5 x 12 = 30 months [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

activities.title: An emergency equipment lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are teaching a private pilot learner in the school's four-seat trainer before his first long cross-country. The lesson covers the ELT, the extinguisher, survival gear and the passenger briefing.

steps.s: At the desk with the aircraft records open, he asks you to just tell him whether the ELT is legal.
options: Tell him; it saves time for the flight
Have him find the inspection entry and battery date and state the rule
Skip it; the school's mechanic tracks the ELT
Tell him to check it on his own some other day
steps.why: He must be able to apply 91.207(c) and (d) himself [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]; in scenario-based training the instructor hands planning to the learner as soon as possible [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

steps.s: Before engine start he briefs you as a passenger: "Belts, doors, and if anything happens, I've got it."
options: Accept it; you are a pilot and know the rest
Give the briefing yourself so it is done right
Tell him briefings are only needed for paying passengers
Ask him to add the extinguisher's location and operation and the survival kit's location and contents
steps.why: The SAFETY list includes the fire extinguisher (location and operation) and the emergency/survival kit (location and contents) [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

steps.s: In cruise you simulate smoke in the cabin. He reaches straight for the cabin air vents.
options: Stop him: extinguisher first, then vents, and close them if smoke grows
Let him; fresh air is the priority
Have him turn off only the avionics master
Have him lower the flaps to slow down first
steps.why: Open the vents only after the extinguisher (if available) is used, and close them at once if smoke increases [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

steps.s: After a firm landing he taxis in and reaches for the mixture to shut down.
options: Let him shut down; the ELT only triggers in crashes
Have him switch the ELT to ON to test it
Have him listen on 121.5 MHz before shutdown
Call the tower to report a possible activation
steps.why: Hard landings have caused false activations; monitor 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown at the end of each flight [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

steps.s: In the debrief he says his survival kit is "in the back somewhere, under the bags."
options: Fine, as long as it is aboard
Have him repack it in one easily reached container matched to the route
Tell him a kit is optional under Part 91, so drop it
Move it to the glare shield for quick access
steps.why: The kit should be assembled in one container that is easily reachable [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]], with equipment for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].
